newsitem.title: USA: EMU divergence trades still viable hedge - analyst.
newsitem.headline: EMU divergence trades still viable hedge - analyst.

text.p: Divergence trades in European fixed income are still a viable part of portfolio strategies despite a generally converging trend ahead of Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), experts said on Wednesday.

There would be bumps on the road, both before and after the 1999 targeted start of EMU, that could easily increase volatility, Pamela Moulton, global co-head of fixed income research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said at an economic forum hosted by the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).

Widening trades in forward rate spreads between mark and Ecu instruments or directional volatility spreads, using put options, might be some safer hedges that would not erode gains from mainstream convergence positions too much, she said.
"They've converged enough even if EMU goes through," she noted, referring to limited risks in forward spreads. "That spread will likely blow out considerably if EMU blows up."
Likewise, implied volatility spreads between options on 10-year German bunds and other high-yielding European bonds had narrowed significantly in the past nine months, she added.

On the whole, Moulton said, "implied EMU probabilities" calculated from swaps spreads showed EMU was on course to create a more unified European bond market bigger than the yen market and about half the size of the U.S. dollar market.
"The difference between these government bonds will be small enough to view the post-EMU market as one government market with slightly different credit ratings," she said.

In the post-EMU era, European spreads would eventually boil down to relative value or credit trades, and portfolio managers looking for lower correlation to diversify would have to turn to emerging markets, she added.
Still, Moulton expected EMU-linked volatility to linger for many more years to come.
German Bundestag elections due next year would be among the early obstacles, she said.
"That's when there's a remote possibility that (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl could get thrown out," she said. "Remote possibility, but I think it could easily add volatility."
The lag between the introduction of a single currency, the Euro, in 1999 and the phasing out of national currencies about three years later was seen as another source of turbulence.
"Once all the national notes and coins are phased out, it will be a lot harder for any individual country to just abandon EMU," she said.
Furthermore, the market, which currently is fixated about who joins the system, would probably begin speculating who would quit once EMU got under way, she added.

Thomas Vear, partner of Rock Futures Group, also told the forum that the linkage between CBOT and London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), which began last May, had made it easier to trade spreads between German bund and U.S. Treasury contracts.

Showing option strategies under several scenarios, Vear said June 1998 expirations were the key contracts in spread trades because they would cover the expected announcement next April/May of the list of countries joining EMU.
